text:
Lightning Weave: Improving the Accuracy-Efficiency Frontier of Reasoning Models through Capability Composition : https://t.co/2pbNev9Ia4

"Yecheng WuMassachusetts Institute of Technologywyc557@mit.eduhttps://github.com/jet-ai-projects/Lightning-WeaveSong HanMassachusetts Institute of TechnologyNVIDIAHan CaiNVIDIA
Abstract
A core goal of efficient reasoning is to improve the accuracy–efficiency frontier. However, jointly improving reasoning accuracy and inference efficiency can be challenging, as the two objectives can favor different reasoning behaviors. Independently post-trained models already offer distinct strengths in accuracy and efficiency. We introduce Lightning Weave, a post-training framework that extracts and composes these independently learned capabilities in a single student through on-policy distillation. Each acquired capability is represented by the policy shift from the model before post-training to the resulting specialist. Lightning Weave combines aligned log-ratio shifts at shared student token states and uses Tilted-Target DOPD to convert the cached signals into a stable learning target. Each anchor pair scores the cached trajectories once, enabling subsequent student training without serving multiple live anchor models concurrently. Across diverse student models and benchmarks in mathematics and code, Lightning Weave substantially improves upon the base students and achieves a state-of-the-art accuracy–efficiency frontier. On Qwen3.5-4B, it raises HMMT 2025 accuracy from 59.2% to 64.0% with 10.7% fewer response tokens, and LiveCodeBench v5 accuracy from 41.7% to 54.2% with 9.6% fewer response tokens. Adjusting the relative strengths of the anchor signals yields a strong empirical accuracy–efficiency Pareto frontier. These results establish Lightning Weave as a new practical route to efficient reasoning through capability composition. Our code is released at https://t.co/K5MCwgyeWK.
📷Figure 1:Left: Intuition of Lightning Weave. Accuracy- and efficiency-oriented anchor pairs isolate complementary capabilities acquired through independent post-training. Lightning Weave composes these capabilities into a joint target, transferring both to a single student and thereby improving its accuracy and efficiency simultaneously. Right: On Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, varying the relative strengths of the two capabilities yields a family of students that traces an empirical accuracy–efficiency Pareto frontier on HMMT 2025. The resulting frontier compares favorably with the base model, single-anchor policies, and existing efficient-reasoning methods.
1Introduction
Large reasoning models have achieved strong performance on complex tasks, but often generate lengthy reasoning traces that incur substantial inference cost. Aggressively shortening these traces can compromise accuracy by curtailing useful exploration. Efficient reasoning therefore aims to improve the accuracy–efficiency frontier, achieving stronger performance for a given inference budget. Existing approaches pursue this goal through length-aware reinforcement learning and fine-tuning (Jiang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2026b), training and distillation across reasoning modes (Luo et al., 2026a; Liang et al., 2026; Ruan et al., 2026), and merging deliberate and concise reasoning models in parameter space (Wu et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025; Lan et al., 2025).Directly optimizing accuracy and efficiency together can be challenging, as the two objectives can favor different reasoning behaviors and improvements in one may compromise the other. Meanwhile, independently post-trained models already offer distinct strengths in reasoning accuracy (Su et al., 2026) and efficiency (Jiang et al., 2026). This suggests a complementary route to efficient reasoning: extract what these specialists have already learned and compose their capabilities in a single student through policy distillation (Rusu et al., 2016). The challenge is to reconcile their potentially competing effects on accuracy and token use within the same reasoning task. This motivates our central question: Can capabilities learned through independent post-training be extracted and composed to improve a student’s accuracy–efficiency frontier?We introduce Lightning Weave, a capability-composition framework built on on-policy distillation (OPD) (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024). OPD supervises a student on its own generated trajectories using a teacher’s token-probability distributions, and recent multi-teacher approaches use this mechanism to integrate specialized capabilities (Ma et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026b; Chen et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026). To represent what each specialist has learned, we follow Direct On-Policy Distillation (DOPD) (Feng et al., 2026) and related policy-shift formulations (Yang et al., 2026a; Yu et al., 2026). We pair each specialist with its checkpoint before the relevant post-training stage, forming an anchor pair. The log-ratio of their token probabilities represents the behavioral shift acquired during post-training. Lightning Weave aligns these shifts in the student’s token space and combines them into one student target, without requiring matching model parameters.Composing multiple shifts online, however, makes supervision costly: with K anchor pairs, each new student rollout requires scoring by up to 2​K anchor models. Lightning OPD (Wu et al., 2026d) demonstrates an offline pipeline that caches teacher feedback before student training, suggesting a practical route to offline composition. Yet directly reusing DOPD’s sampled-token objective on cached trajectories does not generally preserve the intended stationary target. As the student moves away from the behavior policy that generated the cache, the regularizer estimated from cached actions need not equal the intended KL penalty for the current student. Consequently, even after the student reaches the intended shifted policy, the cached surrogate can still produce a non-zero gradient and push the student away from that solution.We address this mismatch with Tilted-Target DOPD. Each cached shift tilts the frozen behavior policy into an explicit target distribution, and training minimizes the KL divergence from the current student to this target. For the token-level DOPD surrogate, this construction preserves the expected initial update and makes the loss and gradient vanish when the student matches the target on cached states. The explicit target thus provides corrective feedback as the student changes, giving offline capability transfer a well-defined stationary solution.Using this objective, Lightning Weave composes the accuracy- and efficiency-oriented shifts at every shared student token state. We first take a weighted sum of the aligned log-ratios and then use it to construct one joint tilted target. Composing shifts before target construction lets all capability sources jointly supervise each student decision. Each anchor pair scores the same cached trajectories once, after which optimization requires only the student and cached scores. Adjusting the relative strengths of the anchor signals yields students with different accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.We evaluate Lightning Weave across diverse student models in separate mathematics and code training settings, covering five benchmarks. Our primary setting composes the accuracy-oriented shift from Klear (Su et al., 2026) with the efficiency-oriented shift from DECS (Jiang et al., 2026). Across the fully evaluated students, composition improves the overall accuracy–efficiency trade-off over the base and either single-anchor alternative. On Qwen3-4B (Yang et al., 2025), Lightning Weave raises AIME 2024 (Mathematical Association of America, 2026) accuracy from 72.9% to 76.0% while reducing response tokens by 21.3%. On Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026), it raises HMMT 2025 (Harvard–MIT Mathematics Tournament, 2025) accuracy from 59.2% to 64.0% with 10.7% fewer response tokens, and LiveCodeBench v5 (Jain et al., 2025) accuracy from 41.7% to 54.2% with 9.6% fewer tokens. Adjusting the relative strengths of the anchor signals during training yields a family of students with a strong empirical accuracy–efficiency Pareto frontier. These results support capability composition as a practical route to more accurate and efficient reasoning.
2Related Work

Efficient Reasoning.
Efficient reasoning improves the accuracy–efficiency frontier by controlling inference computation. Existing approaches regulate token budgets and prune low-confidence traces (Han et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2025c), optimize length-aware objectives (Luo et al., 2026b; Aggarwal and Welleck, 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2026), compress chain-of-thought traces (Xia et al., 2025), or reason in continuous representations (Hao et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). Others train or distill adaptive and budget-controlled reasoning modes (Luo et al., 2026a; Liang et al., 2026; Ruan et al., 2026), or merge deliberate and concise checkpoints (Wu et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025; Lan et al., 2025). Systems-oriented approaches include reward-guided and step-level speculation (Liao et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2025b), certainty-guided allocation and scheduling in Dynasor (Fu et al., 2025a), and KV-cache compression in R-KV and SkipKV (Cai et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2026). These methods target generated tokens, latency, memory, and throughput. Lightning Weave targets the student’s accuracy–efficiency frontier through post-training capability composition, complementing inference-time systems optimization.
Capability Composition.
Capabilities can be integrated through policy distillation and knowledge amalgamation (Rusu et al., 2016; Parisotto et al., 2016; Teh et al., 2017; You et al., 2017; Shen et al., 2019a; Shen et al., 2019b), heterogeneous output-space fusion (Wan et al., 2024), or parameter-space model merging (Li et al., 2022; Wortsman et al., 2022; Matena and Raffel, 2022; Ilharco et al., 2023; Yadav et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024a; Yu et al., 2024). Multi-objective alignment studies reward-specialized interpolation and controllable trade-offs (Rame et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024b; Zhong et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2024), while multi-teacher OPD integrates domain specialists and mitigates capability interference (Ma et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026b; Chen et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026). Rather than merging endpoint parameters or directly matching specialist policies, Lightning Weave composes aligned post-training policy shifts at shared student token states. This decouples composition from parameter compatibility while reconciling independently learned accuracy and efficiency capabilities within the same reasoning task.
On-Policy Distillation.
OPD provides dense teacher supervision on student-generated trajectories (Gu et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2024; Lu and Lab, 2025; Song and Zheng, 2026). Recent work analyzes its failure modes (Li et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2026; Armandpour et al., 2026), refines optimization (Ko et al., 2026; Jin et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026b), and enables cross-tokenizer transfer (He et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a). DOPD and related formulations transfer policy shifts through teacher–reference log-ratios or positive–negative model contrasts (Yang et al., 2026a; Feng et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026). Lightning OPD caches teacher feedback for offline training, while Lightning OPD 2.0 corrects cross-teacher style bias (Wu et al., 2026d; Wu et al., 2026c). Building on policy-shift supervision and offline caching, Tilted-Target DOPD provides an explicit, stable learning target on cached student states, enabling capability composition without serving multiple live anchor models during student training.
3Method
We develop Lightning Weave to improve the accuracy–efficiency frontier by composing independently learned capabilities in a single student. As illustrated in Figure 2, we represent each capability as an anchor-pair policy shift, align these shifts at shared student-generated token states, and compose them into a joint learning target. We first review OPD and policy-shift supervision, then introduce Tilted-Target DOPD to provide an explicit, stable target for offline capability transfer, and finally build multi-anchor composition on this foundation.📷Figure 2:Overview of Lightning Weave. (1) Capability-specific policy shifts. Given a prompt, the frozen behavior policy generates a rollout whose token states are shared by all independently trained anchor pairs. The log-ratio between each post-trained anchor and its pre-anchor isolates the corresponding capability-specific policy shift. (2) Statewise multi-anchor composition. Lightning Weave combines the weighted shifts at every token state, allowing compatible changes to reinforce one another while reconciling competing changes locally. (3) Tilted-target distillation. The composed shift exponentially tilts the behavior policy into an explicit target distribution, which the student learns through KL minimization.

3.1Preliminaries
ℒOPD(θ)=𝔼x∼𝒟,y^∼πθ[∑tDKL(πθ(⋅∣st)∥πT(⋅∣st))].(1)Let x∼𝒟 be a prompt, y^∼πθ(⋅∣x) a student response, and st=(x,y^<t) its token-level state. Given a teacher πT, standard OPD minimizes the KL to the teacher on student-generated states (Agarwal et al., 2024):Direct On-Policy Distillation (DOPD) (Feng et al., 2026) instead represents a specialist with a post-trained anchor and its pre-anchor, denoted by (π+,π−). The sequence-level policy shift decomposes into dense token-level rewards:Δ⁡(y^∣x)=log⁡π+​(y^∣x)π−​(y^∣x)=∑trΔ​(y^t∣st),rΔ​(a∣s)=log⁡π+​(a∣s)π−​(a∣s).(2)This ratio isolates the behavioral change introduced by post-training rather than the endpoint policy π+. Let πb denote the initial student. In its idealized sequence-level form, DOPD maximizes𝒥DOPD(θ)=𝔼x∼𝒟[𝔼y^∼πθ(⋅∣x)[Δ(y^∣x)]−αDKL(πθ(⋅∣x)∥πb(⋅∣x))],(3)where α>0 controls the KL penalty. Following DOPD’s zero-discount token-level surrogate, we use rΔ​(a∣s) as the immediate reward at each visited state.
3.2Single-Anchor Distillation: Tilted-Target DOPD

Offline DOPD and its limitation.
Online DOPD must serve both anchors to evaluate rΔ on the states visited by the current student. Inspired by offline score caching (Wu et al., 2026d), we instead sample trajectories once from πb and cache their anchor shifts. Let dπb denote the resulting token-state distribution. A naive cached surrogate for Eq. 3 is𝒥naive(θ)=𝔼s∼dπb[𝔼a∼πθ(⋅∣s)[rΔ(a∣s)]−αD^KLb(πθ(⋅∣s)∥πb(⋅∣s))],(4)where D^KLb denotes DOPD’s low-variance sampled-token KL estimator evaluated on a cached action ab∼πb(⋅∣s). In particular, D^KLb=exp⁡(ℓθ)−1−ℓθ, where ℓθ=log⁡πb​(ab∣s)−log⁡πθ​(ab∣s). At initialization, the cached states and actions are on-policy, so Eq. 4 matches the online DOPD update. As πθ departs from πb, however, cached actions no longer yield an on-policy estimate of the KL regularizer. The regularization is therefore not guaranteed to cancel the fixed policy-shift update at the intended solution, allowing training to continue pushing after the shift has been absorbed. The cached states remain an offline approximation; our correction instead restores a well-defined fixed point on these states.
Tilted-Target DOPD.
We make the destination of the regularized update explicit. Using the full-distribution form, each cached state s∼dπb definesq(⋅∣s)=argmaxπ{𝔼a∼π(⋅∣s)[rΔ(a∣s)]−αDKL(π(⋅∣s)∥πb(⋅∣s))},q⁡(a∣s)=πb​(a∣s)​exp⁡(rΔ​(a∣s)/α)Z⁡(s).(5)Here Z⁡(s)=∑aπb​(a∣s)​exp⁡(rΔ​(a∣s)/α) normalizes the distribution over actions. A larger α keeps q closer to πb, while a smaller α applies a stronger anchor shift. We then use the same student-to-target KL form as OPD, evaluated on the cached states:ℒTT(θ)=α𝔼s∼dπb[DKL(πθ(⋅∣s)∥q(⋅∣s))].(6)Substituting Eq. 5 givesαDKL(πθ∥q)=αDKL(πθ∥πb)−𝔼a∼πθ[rΔ(a∣s)]+αlogZ(s).(7)Because log⁡Z⁡(s) is independent of θ, Eq. 6 is equivalent to the full-distribution, KL-regularized DOPD objective on each cached state. It preserves the expected per-state online update at initialization and, unlike the naive surrogate, has an explicit fixed point: the loss and gradient vanish when πθ=q. Repeated optimization therefore approaches a well-defined policy target rather than continually extrapolating the cached shift. This self-correcting behavior stabilizes offline training.
3.3Multi-Anchor Distillation: Lightning Weave

Aligned policy-shift composition.
Having established stable transfer from one anchor pair, we now seek a single student target that realizes the changes acquired by K independently trained specialists. The i-th pair (πi+,πi−) induces the token-level shift ri​(a∣s)=log⁡πi+​(a∣s)πi−​(a∣s). We evaluate every pair on the same states cached from πb and express its scores over a common student action space. At each student decision, the resulting {ri​(a∣s)}i=1K therefore describe how different post-training procedures reweight the same action distribution. Because these changes are expressed as log-density ratios, their weighted composition isr𝐰(a∣s)=∑i=1Kwiri(a∣s)=log∏i=1K(πi+​(a∣s)πi−​(a∣s))wi,(8)where 𝐰=(w1,…,wK) contains non-negative capability weights that satisfy ∑i=1Kwi=1. Their values determine the balance among capabilities, and we use wi=1/K for equal composition. With the same α and optimization configuration, setting one weight to one and all others to zero exactly recovers the corresponding single-anchor objective.
Lightning Weave.
We apply the composed shift once to the common behavior policy, definingq𝐰(⋅∣s)=argmaxπ{𝔼a∼π(⋅∣s)[r𝐰(a∣s)]−αDKL(π(⋅∣s)∥πb(⋅∣s))}.(9)The objective is strictly concave in π and has the unique solutionq𝐰​(a∣s)=πb​(a∣s)Z𝐰​(s)​exp⁡(1α​∑i=1Kwi​ri​(a∣s))=πb​(a∣s)Z𝐰​(s)​∏i=1K(πi+​(a∣s)πi−​(a∣s))wi/α.(10)Here Z𝐰​(s)=∑aπb​(a∣s)​exp⁡(r𝐰​(a∣s)/α) normalizes q𝐰 over the common student action space. Equation 10 is a product of relative policy changes around one shared student prior, not an arithmetic mixture of teacher distributions. Anchor pairs that support the same action reinforce one another, while conflicting changes are reconciled locally through their weighted ratios. In the sample-mixing baseline, each example is supervised by only one anchor-specific target, leaving their interaction implicit in shared model parameters; our construction specifies that interaction directly at every aligned token state. We then fit the student to this joint target usingℒjoint(θ;𝐰)=α𝔼s∼dπb[DKL(πθ(⋅∣s)∥q𝐰(⋅∣s))].(11)Expanding this KL shows that, up to a θ-independent constant, the objective combines the weighted DOPD directions under a single KL constraint, while its loss and gradient vanish at q𝐰. Equation 11 recovers Tilted-Target DOPD when K=1. Each anchor pair is scored only once; after the aligned shifts are cached, training serves only the student regardless of the number of anchors. Complete derivations are provided in Appendix A, and practical finite-target approximation and cross-tokenizer alignment are described in Appendix B.4.

text:
106-year-old Red Army veteran recalls the Long March #LongMarch90 

My name is Zhao Maolin. I was born in April 1920 in Daxian county, southwest China's Sichuan Province, now part of Dachuan district in Dazhou. I'm 106 years old.

My parents died when I was young. In 1934, at just 14, I joined the Red Army. The following year, I set out on the Long March.

I served as a medic. Over the years, I have traveled many roads, but nothing compares with the hardships of crossing snow-capped mountains and vast marshlands.

Jiajin Mountain, for example, was notoriously difficult to cross. Beneath the snow lay hidden sheets of ice, making the mountain paths very slippery. Every step took enormous effort, and one wrong move could send a person tumbling down the slope.

I was small and had short legs, so climbing was especially difficult. The higher we went, the thinner the air became, and my body shook uncontrollably from the cold and exhaustion.

The weather in the mountains could change in an instant. Howling winds whipped snow and ice into our faces. When the wind died down, sunlight reflecting off the snow was so intense that it hurt our eyes. Our thin, coarse-cloth uniforms offered little protection against the bitter cold. Snow settled on our clothes and melted, only to freeze again, leaving the fabric stiff as a shell of ice.

Along the way, fallen comrades lay beneath the snow, their outlines still visible. But we could not stop. Anyone who sat down risked never getting back up.

Beyond the mountains lay the marshlands, another deadly obstacle. Beneath the grassy surface were pools of dark, stagnant water. In some places, the water reached our knees. In others, it was deep enough to swallow a person whole. We had to move cautiously, following the footprints of those ahead and stepping only on patches of tangled grass roots.

Many comrades never made it out alive.

Our food supplies soon ran out. When we stopped to camp, we searched for grass roots and wild greens, boiling them into a soup to stave off hunger.

One veteran soldier handed me half a handful of highland barley. As a medic, I could not bring myself to eat the barley. Instead, I boiled it into thin porridge and shared it with wounded and sick comrades, giving each person just a small mouthful.

After surviving the snow-capped mountains and marshlands and coming through so many life-and-death ordeals, the hardships that lay ahead no longer seemed insurmountable.

In 1942, I joined the Communist Party of China (CPC). After the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, I transferred to a civilian post in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region and retired in 1981.

Retirement hasn't dulled the resolve the Long March gave me, not for a moment. In idle hours, I often think of the comrades who remain in the snowy mountains and marshlands, and of that journey where survival was never certain.

text:
Krishna 

The god who chose to be a charioteer, and the voice that turned doubt into dharma

Some heroes in the Mahabharata wield weapons.
Some wield kingdoms.
Krishna wields something far greater: the power to change hearts without raising a hand.
Born in a prison, raised in a village of cowherds, and destined to become the most influential figure of his age, Krishna’s life defies every convention. He is a prince of the Yadavas, yet he grows up among simple folk in Gokul and Vrindavan. He is a warrior of immense skill, yet he chooses not to fight in the Kurukshetra war. He is a god in human form, yet he lives, loves, and suffers as a man.
When the Pandavas are exiled and the war becomes inevitable, Krishna plays the role of diplomat. He travels to Hastinapura as a peace envoy, offering Duryodhana a compromise: give the Pandavas just five villages, and war can be avoided. Duryodhana refuses, famously declaring he will not give even land the size of a needle’s tip. Krishna returns with the knowledge that war is now unavoidable.

On the eve of battle, Krishna offers both sides a choice: he will not fight, but they may have either his army or himself. Duryodhana, ever the strategist, chooses the army. Arjuna chooses Krishna—and in doing so, chooses the path of dharma.

Krishna becomes Arjuna’s charioteer, a role that seems humble for a king and a god. But it is in this role that he delivers the epic’s most sacred teaching: the Bhagavad Gita.

As the two armies face each other, Arjuna sees his elders, his teachers, his cousins on the other side. Overwhelmed by grief and moral confusion, he drops his bow and refuses to fight. Krishna does not scold him. He does not command him. Instead, he speaks.

He explains the nature of the soul—eternal, unborn, indestructible.
He explains the nature of duty—how action must be performed without attachment to results.
He explains the nature of dharma—how righteousness is not always comfortable, but always necessary.
And finally, he reveals his true form: the cosmic, infinite Vishvarupa, in which all creation begins and ends.

Arjuna’s doubt dissolves. He picks up his bow. The war begins.

Throughout the eighteen days of battle, Krishna guides Arjuna not just as a charioteer, but as a strategist, a protector, and a moral compass. He steers the chariot away from danger, offers counsel in moments of doubt, and ensures that dharma prevails—even when it requires difficult choices. He does not fight, but his presence changes everything.
After the war, Krishna’s role does not end. He witnesses the grief, the guilt, and the slow unraveling of the Yadava clan. He sees the curse that will destroy his own people and the submersion of Dwarka into the sea. He accepts it all with the same calm he showed on the battlefield, knowing that even gods must yield to the flow of time.
Krishna’s story is a meditation on:
The nature of duty—how action must be performed without attachment to outcomes.

The role of the guide—not to fight your battles, but to help you see clearly.

The paradox of divinity—how the infinite can choose to be humble.

In the Mahabharata’s vast cast of kings, warriors, and sages, Krishna stands apart:
The god who chose to be a servant.
The teacher who spoke only when asked.
The friend who stood by dharma, even when it demanded everything.

text:
U.S. Army Sergeant Charles Robert Jenkins, who deserted his post and crossed into North Korea in January 1965...

In January 1965, 24-year-old Jenkins was on patrol near the Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ). Fearing he would be sent to fight in the Vietnam War, he walked across the border into North Korea, expecting to seek asylum in the Soviet Union and eventually return home. Instead of being freed, he was held by North Korean authorities for 39 years, 6 months, and 4 days. During this time, he was subjected to harsh living conditions, forced indoctrination, physical abuse, and appeared as an "evil American" villain in North Korean propaganda films.

. . . 

An American soldier crossed into North Korea believing he would eventually find his way home. On January 5, 1965, Sergeant Charles Robert Jenkins deserted his unit near the Korean Demilitarized Zone and walked toward North Korean territory carrying a rifle with a white cloth attached to it. He feared dangerous patrols and the possibility of being sent to fight in Vietnam. His plan, as he later explained, was to seek help through the Soviet embassy and arrange his return to the United States. Instead, North Korean authorities detained him, beginning almost forty years of life under a government he had badly misunderstood.

Jenkins was 24 and serving with the United States Army in South Korea. Korean War had ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty, and the border separating the two Koreas remained heavily militarized. Patrols near the frontier were dangerous, while the expanding American involvement in Vietnam created additional anxiety among soldiers. Jenkins later admitted drinking heavily before making his decision. His fears were real, but his intended solution rested on a disastrous misunderstanding. He imagined that communist North Korea might offer a temporary refuge from which he could eventually return to civilian life. He had little understanding of how the country treated foreigners who entered its territory.

North Korean soldiers took him into custody, and the hoped-for journey to Soviet embassy never materialized. Jenkins was interrogated and placed under constant supervision. He eventually lived alongside three other American servicemen who had crossed into North Korea: James Dresnok, Jerry Parrish and Larry Abshier. Men were subjected to political indoctrination, restricted movement and demands of a government that regarded them as propaganda assets. In his later memoir, Jenkins described shortages, beatings and psychological pressure. His recollections must be distinguished from independently documented facts, but his prolonged confinement and use in propaganda are well established.

North Korean government put Americans to work teaching English and appearing in films. Their foreign appearance made them useful as characters representing hostile Americans in state productions. Jenkins became recognizable to some North Korean audiences through these roles, even though his freedom remained severely restricted. He had exchanged the possibility of military service in Vietnam for life in a country where he could not decide where to live or travel. Years passed without an opportunity to return home. American authorities classified him as a deserter, while his relatives struggled to understand what had happened to him.

His circumstances changed in 1980 when North Korean officials introduced him to Hitomi Soga, a Japanese woman who had been abducted by North Korean agents in 1978. Soga had been taken from Japan with her mother, whose fate remains unresolved. She and Jenkins shared the experience of living in a foreign country without the freedom to leave. They married and eventually had two daughters
(Mika and Brinda). Their relationship gave Jenkins a family, but it also created another reason to fear separation. The children grew up in North Korea, and their parents had to consider how any attempt to escape might affect them.

text:
#UdtaTeer Full Review - #CinemaWithParth 

Udta Teer is a below-average film that squanders a promising premise through uneven writing, an inconsistent screenplay and an inability to decide what it wants to be. The film has the ingredients for an entertaining political spoof, but its execution rarely lives up to that potential. Several sequences are unnecessarily stretched, the narrative lacks pace, and the overall experience leaves little impact. Even the three songs are thoroughly mediocre, none memorable enough to stay with me once the film ends.

Biggest issue with the film is its tonal inconsistency. For most of its runtime, I watched it as a spoof, expecting irreverent humour and a satirical take on its subject. However, the climax suddenly seems to demand that I take the proceedings seriously. There is nothing inherently wrong with blending parody and drama, but the transition needs to be earned. Here, it feels as though the film itself is uncertain about its intentions. Even if I set aside the plot's implausibilities and surrender to its absurdity, the humour remains frustratingly inconsistent. Some jokes land, but a substantial portion falls flat, leaving me acutely aware of the punchline without actually laughing.

The film's treatment of its premise is particularly disappointing because there was considerable scope for a sharper, more cohesive satire. The mockery of Pakistan's ISI and Army occasionally works, but the screenplay struggles to sustain that irreverence. The political references, including those invoking Operation Sindoor, sometimes feel inserted rather than organically integrated into the narrative. A spoof need not adhere to realism, but it does need a coherent comic sensibility. Udta Teer frequently mistakes the absurdity of a situation for the effectiveness of the joke.

Ayushmann Khurrana is hit and miss. He has moments where his comic timing works, but there are stretches where his performance feels surprisingly flat. The problem isn't entirely his, though, because even a capable performer can do only so much with material that lacks consistency. The supporting cast offers occasional moments of amusement, but the writing doesn't extract enough from its ensemble. The second half is especially culpable, dragging through stretches that needed sharper editing and greater narrative urgency. The climax twist is genuinely effective and provides a brief glimpse of what the film might have achieved with a more disciplined screenplay.

The post-credit scene, meanwhile, presents an interesting what-if. What if that revelation had been positioned as the actual climax instead? It might have given the narrative a more compelling direction, or at least a more satisfying payoff. As presented, however, it feels less like a genuine twist and more like an idea that could have been developed into something substantially better. That said, I don't want to dismiss everything the film gets right. There are comic portions that work, the political satire occasionally finds its mark, and the climax has merit. These moments, however, remain isolated successes rather than parts of a consistently engaging film.

What I find equally disheartening is the apparent proliferation of influencer accounts handing out four-star ratings using strikingly similar wording. If these endorsements are paid promotions presented as independent reviews, they do a disservice to audiences who rely on critics to make informed viewing decisions. A four-star verdict does not become credible merely because several accounts repeat the same adjectives. Such practices risk eroding the credibility of these reviewers while reducing film criticism to a marketing exercise. And reviewing a film without even watching it is worse still. It is not criticism; it is a disingenuous performance masquerading as one. Film reviewing demands independent judgment, intellectual honesty and a willingness to acknowledge both a film's merits and its failures. Without those principles, the entire art of reviewing is diminished.

Udta Teer has a promising premise, a handful of effective comic moments and a worthwhile climax, but its uneven humour, muddled tonal identity, stretched second half and forgettable music ultimately make it a disappointing experience. I came away feeling that the film had the ingredients for something considerably better but lacked the clarity and craftsmanship to bring them together. A few good moments cannot compensate for a film that never quite figures out what it wants to say, or how it wants to say it.

🇮🇳🎯 NAGASTRA-2 CLEARS TECHNICAL TRIALS, DELIVERY TO INDIAN ARMY BEGINS...
India’s indigenous defence manufacturing receives a boost as Solar Defence & Aerospace Ltd begins deliveries of the Nagastra-2 loitering munition to the Indian Army following successful technical trials at Mahajan Field Firing Range in August 2026.
Equipped with day-and-night electro-optical and infrared (EO/IR) surveillance capabilities, Nagastra-2 features a 4 kg tandem shaped-charge warhead with a reported penetration capability of 650 mm of rolled homogeneous armour (RHA). According to the specifications provided, the system offers a range of 25 km in recover-and-reuse mode and up to 50 km in fire-and-forget mode, with an endurance of 60 minutes.
The system also incorporates electronic counter-countermeasures (ECCM) designed to counter communication and GPS jamming or spoofing, along with encrypted video and telemetry links. With more than 80% indigenous content, Nagastra-2 reflects India’s ongoing efforts to strengthen domestic defence manufacturing and reduce reliance on foreign systems.

Three days to crawl five kilometers: Ukrainian troops reveal how they fought Russia inside an underground gas pipeline near Kupiansk.

Ukrainian assault troops spent weeks fighting inside a narrow underground gas pipeline near Kupiansk, crawling through mud and darkness, establishing defensive positions and engaging Russian forces attempting to use the infrastructure as a concealed route into the strategically important city in northeastern Ukraine. 

The operation, carried out by the 425th Separate Assault Regiment, known as Skelya @skelya425, was given a fitting name by the soldiers who participated in it: Operation Impossible.

In video testimony released by the regiment👇, Ukrainian soldiers described an extraordinary battlefield where conventional infantry tactics had to be adapted to an environment barely large enough for a person to move through. 

The pipeline, measuring approximately 100 to 110 centimeters (39 to 43 inches) in diameter, forced troops to crawl or move on their knees for extended periods while carrying weapons, ammunition and other equipment. One soldier recalled that reaching his assigned position required traveling five kilometers through the pipeline, a journey that took approximately three days.

Conditions underground were severe. Soldiers described cold, damp sections of the pipeline, standing water, thick mud, poor air quality and debris that complicated movement and made even basic tasks exhausting. Groups of roughly 10 men moved in single file through the confined space, while supplies and equipment had to be transported along the same restricted route. The soldiers also encountered the remains of Russian troops inside the pipeline, adding to the physical and psychological demands of an operation conducted almost entirely in darkness.

The mission was to prevent Russian forces from exploiting the underground infrastructure to infiltrate Kupiansk. According to Skelya, Russian troops had been using the gas pipeline to move personnel covertly toward the city, bypassing some of the risks associated with movement across terrain exposed to Ukrainian aerial reconnaissance. Ukrainian assault teams were ordered to enter the pipeline, establish positions and clear enemy forces from the contested sections, while other units maintained defensive positions near the village of Ridkivka to prevent Russian troops from using an entrance farther north.

The fighting developed into a prolonged struggle for control of the underground passage. Ukrainian soldiers described Russian positions protected by several layers of sandbags, with opposing forces at times separated by as little as 20 meters. Cameras and other observation equipment were used to monitor enemy activity, while Ukrainian troops established machine-gun positions to prevent Russian soldiers from advancing through the confined space. Explosives were also used to block sections of the pipeline and deny the enemy access to parts of the underground route.

One of the more unusual aspects of the operation was the use of small battery-powered vehicles to transport personnel through the pipeline. Soldiers described electric carts fitted with motors, wheels and controls that allowed them to travel in either direction, with some reportedly capable of carrying about 10 people. The improvised transportation system helped overcome the enormous distances involved in underground movement, although soldiers still faced lengthy journeys through sections where crawling was the only option. One participant compared riding the carts through the darkness to a roller coaster, while another described spending more than five days unable to leave the pipeline after suffering an injury.

For the soldiers, the physical demands of the operation were as memorable as the fighting itself. One participant said the journey back to the surface took approximately a day and a half, following an extended period in which he had been forced to remain almost constantly in a horizontal position. When asked what he wanted most after emerging from the pipeline, his answer was strikingly simple: to stand upright again.

According to the regiment, Ukrainian forces spent approximately two months conducting operations inside the gas pipeline, eventually clearing several kilometers of the underground route and preventing Russian troops from continuing to use the contested section to infiltrate Kupiansk. The fighting was not simply about securing a piece of industrial infrastructure. It was part of the broader battle to control the approaches to the city and deny Russian forces concealed routes for moving personnel toward Ukrainian defensive positions.

Operation Impossible also provides another example of how the proliferation of drones is reshaping ground warfare in Ukraine. Persistent aerial reconnaissance and precision strikes have made movement across open terrain increasingly dangerous, encouraging both sides to search for alternative routes that offer concealment. Industrial infrastructure, including underground pipelines, can provide such routes, but the advantages of avoiding observation come with severe restrictions on movement, communication, logistics and evacuation. Once opposing forces enter the same underground passage, the resulting combat can take place at distances of only a few dozen meters, with little room to maneuver.

The disclosure follows another Ukrainian underground operation near Kupiansk, known as Operation Veles, in which the 2nd National Guard Corps, Khartiia, reported using more than 15 kilometers of underground routes to reach Russian rear positions and conduct a counteroffensive. 

Together, the operations demonstrate how the battlefield is expanding beyond the traditional dimensions of ground and air combat. As drones increasingly restrict movement on the surface, underground infrastructure is becoming both a means of maneuver and an objective worth fighting over.

Source: Ukraine’s 425th Separate Assault Regiment @Skelya425, October 23, 2026.

text:
Commit or Abstain? System One Decision Models, LLMs, and Missing Legal Authority : https://t.co/h3IWlblwcw

"M. Mikail DemirDepartment of Information Science, University at Albany, SUNY, Albany, NY, USAmdemir@albany.edu
© none
Abstract.
Given the enormous number of claims to be checked, verifiable legal AI requires scalable, cost-effective models that answer the practical needs of law. System One decision models are built on large language models but, instead of generating text, return a calibrated probability for each option. This suits the verification of legal authority, where the question is closed: a given holding, or none of them. We test whether such models abstain when the correct authority is missing. We extend CaseHOLD with an abstention condition in which the correct holding is replaced in 1,670 of 5,314 items, and compare four decision models with six generative LLMs. When no option is correct, generative LLMs still pick one in 38–86% of items; the most cautious decision model does so in 30%. On standard CaseHOLD, a decision model matches the best generative LLM (88.1% vs. 88.2%) at 1/55 of the cost. Accepting that LLM’s answer only when a decision model agrees halves its wrong citations, and distilling a decision model’s probabilities into Qwen3-8B, without labels, yields a well-calibrated local model. Legal AI should be judged by its wrong citations, not by accuracy alone.
legal AI, CaseHOLD, calibration, abstention, decision models, knowledge distillationKeywords:

“Resolve to be honest at all events; and if in your own judgment you cannot be an honest lawyer, resolve to be honest without being a lawyer.”
— Abraham Lincoln, Notes for a Law Lecture (c. 1850)

1.Introduction
Figure 1.When the correct authority is missing, most models still cite one. (a) A CaseHOLD item whose true holding was replaced by a similar holding from another case (C); every generative LLM chose it. (b) Share of the 1,670 such items in which each model picked a holding instead of abstaining, against cost per 1,000 questions. System One models are the four cheapest and include the most cautious; among generative LLMs, more spending does not reliably buy caution.
(a) The correct holding is removed
“…It is not the province of this Court, at this stage, to introduce a remedy that in hindsight appears better for the appellant as a matter of equity. See, e.g., In re Bernal, 207 F.3d 595 (9th Cir. 2000) (<HOLDING>)”
A. …the fourth amendment remedy sought is suppressionB. …the remedy in a prison conditions case must remedy actual injuries…C. …no legitimate basis for distinction may be found between the situation where the claim is not timely raised and where the remedy sought was not timely pursuedD. …retroactive award of benefits proper remedy…E. …rendition is remedy for no evidenceF. None of these (correct)
All six LLMs: CThree of four System One models: F(b) How often models still pick a holdingLanguage models are now used across legal practice, and most visibly in legal research. Law has also become one of the best-documented domains of their failure. Since late 2022, courts have sanctioned lawyers and pro se litigants for filings that cite authorities that do not exist or do not support the propositions they are cited for (Mata, 2023; Billups, 2025). Each such filing adds work to an already overburdened court system. Someone has to check the citations, and courts must then hold hearings and decide on sanctions. The problem now reaches the bench, with judges’ own orders among the documented cases (Charlotin, 2026).The problem is not limited to general-purpose chatbots. In a preregistered evaluation, commercial legal research tools built on retrieval-augmented generation, some marketed as hallucination-free, still hallucinated on 17% to 33% of queries (Magesh et al., 2025); general-purpose models did so at least 58% of the time (Dahl et al., 2024). Courts now see the same failure in practice. In October 2026, a federal court reviewed filings whose author admitted taking propositions from a Westlaw AI tool without confirming them (Mercante, 2026). Nor is the problem fading with newer models. Across eight generations of ChatGPT models, citation hallucination rates did not consistently decline, and GPT-5.1 produced hallucinated citations more often than the best mid-2024 GPT-4o release (Liu et al., 2026).Institutions are responding. California requires its courts to adopt generative-AI use policies that address hallucinated output (Judicial Council of California, 2025), and the State Bar of California has proposed amending its rule on candor to the tribunal so that lawyers must verify that cited authorities exist and are accurate (State Bar of California, 2026). Texas has proposed that signers of filings represent that their citations, quotations, and holdings are not fabricated (Supreme Court of Texas, 2026). Appellate courts now sanction unverified citations with fees, fines, and referrals to the bar (Noland, 2025; Whiting, 2026). Yet the cases keep growing, and one public tracker lists 2,203 court matters involving AI hallucinations, 1,264 of them from 2026 alone (Charlotin, 2026). Fabrication is only part of the problem. In 933 of these matters, a real authority was cited for a proposition it does not support (Charlotin, 2026).Technical responses mostly add more language-model machinery: retrieval augmentation, better training data, model editing, decoding strategies (Huang et al., 2025), and agentic verification. These efforts work against a structural pressure. Kalai et al. (2025) trace hallucinations to a simple classification problem, deciding whether a statement is valid. Models make errors on this problem, and the errors persist because training and evaluation reward guessing. Under accuracy-style scoring, a model that always guesses scores higher than one that admits it is unsure. In legal writing, the guess is the costly outcome, a confident citation to the wrong authority. Legal studies observe the same tendency. When told to stop if no factual basis existed, most models produced arguments anyway (Zhang et al., 2025).Most evaluations ask whether a model picks the right authority from a set of candidates, but in practice the right authority is often not among them. A useful system should then say so rather than choose the closest option. We therefore ask whether a model, when the correct authority is missing, commits to a wrong one or abstains. The two errors are not equally costly. A wrong commitment can reach a filing; an unnecessary abstention costs a lawyer an extra lookup. Accuracy treats them the same. What matters instead is whether a model’s confidence can tell a user which answers to https://t.co/ao0B1xVV65 NLP posed many of these problems as classification well before large language models. CaseHOLD asks which of five holdings a court gave for a cited case (Zheng et al., 2021); ContractNLI asks whether a contract entails, contradicts, or does not mention a hypothesis (Koreeda and Manning, 2021); MAUD poses expert questions about merger agreements (Wang et al., 2023). These tasks were addressed with fine-tuned encoders. Since large language models arrived, the same tasks are mostly posed to general-purpose generative models.The underlying need has not changed. Lawyers and courts need to check, at scale, whether a specific authority supports a specific proposition, and to be told when it does not. This calls for precision and calibrated confidence more than open-ended reasoning. A verification model should decide only when the evidence is sufficient (Atanasova et al., 2022), and small models trained for a narrow verification task can match GPT-4 at a fraction of its cost (Tang et al., 2024). If more reasoning alone solved the problem, the strongest models would not continue to hallucinate (Liu et al., 2026). In legal case-based reasoning, reasoning models even spend more computation on wrong answers than on right ones (Zhang et al., 2026b).System One decision models revisit the classification framing with modern models. TypeSafe released the first of them, Jev, in September 2026 (TypeSafe, 2026a). The name follows the fast, intuitive System 1 of Kahneman (2011), and commentators soon began calling them decision models (Willison, 2026). They are themselves built on large language models, but instead of generating text they return a typed decision and a probability for each option. By late September, an analysis of GitHub found 2,170 public projects using Jev (Ling et al., 2026), and a community index now tracks more than 170 decision models from many developers (multimodalart and contributors, 2026). This design fits the task of checking an authority well. The question is closed (this holding, or none of them), so there is nothing to write, and the probability states how sure the model is, which is what a user needs in order to decide what to check. TypeSafe trains its Jev model with reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions (RLCD), which optimizes these probabilities against outcomes rather than human preferences (TypeSafe, 2026b). Whether such models are more trustworthy than generative LLMs where it matters most in law, when the right authority is not available, has not been tested.We examine this with CaseHOLD. We add a condition in which the correct holding is sometimes replaced by a similar holding from another case, and a sixth option states that none of the holdings applies. We compare four System One decision models with six generative LLMs on all 5,314 test items. We ask how often each model commits to a holding when none is correct, what its caution costs, and whether the two kinds of model can cover for each other.Our contributions are:
•A test of abstention for legal authority. We extend CaseHOLD so that in 1,670 of its 5,314 test items the correct holding is replaced by a similar holding from another case, and measure how often a model cites a holding when none applies (Figure 1a).
•A comparison across model types and prices. We evaluate four System One decision models and six generative LLMs from five vendors, reporting accuracy, calibration, abstention, and cost (Figure 1b).
•A cost-aware view of combining them. We show how pairing a System One model with a generative LLM trades wrong citations against items sent for human review, and frame the choice of operating point by the unequal cost of the two errors.
•Local deployment and checks on what the results mean. Trained only on a System One model’s probabilities, with no labeled data, a local Qwen3-8B model learns to answer and abstain like its teacher and becomes well calibrated. Contamination tests extending Arvin (2025) show that models know much of the case law but do not depend on it.Code, data, and the outputs of every model are available at https://t.co/roimS1thAI.
2.Related Work

https://t.co/bfoHyuURyK Datasets with Verifiable Answers
Legal NLP has a long line of datasets whose answers can be checked against a source. Many of them come from contracts. ContractNLI asks whether a contract entails, contradicts, or says nothing about a hypothesis (Koreeda and Manning, 2021), CUAD marks the clauses lawyers look for in contract review (Hendrycks et al., 2021), and MAUD asks expert questions about merger agreements (Wang et al., 2023). COLIEE has run shared tasks on retrieving and entailing statutes and case law for years (Goebel et al., 2024). In CaseHOLD, the dataset we use, a model picks which of five holdings a court gave for a cited case (Zheng et al., 2021); Section 3 describes it in detail. LexGLUE (Chalkidis et al., 2022) and LegalBench (Guha et al., 2023) later gathered tasks like these into suites for evaluating language models, and LawBench did the same for Chinese law (Fei et al., 2024). In almost all of them, the correct answer is among the candidates and every error counts the same. Neither is true when a lawyer checks a citation.
2.2.Abstention and Unanswerable Questions
Outside law, SQuAD 2.0 added questions that look answerable but are not, so that a system had to learn when to stay silent (Rajpurkar et al., 2018). Later work asked the same of language models with multiple-choice questions. Models lose much of their accuracy when none of the above is the right option (Tam et al., 2025), and they keep choosing an option even when every option is wrong (Góral et al., 2025). Across twenty datasets, AbstentionBench even finds that reasoning fine-tuning can make abstention worse (Kirichenko et al., 2025). Kalai et al. (2025) argue that this follows from how models are graded, since a guess is rewarded over an admission of uncertainty. Our abstain condition brings this test to legal authority, where a confident guess becomes a citation to the wrong holding.
2.3.System One Decision Models
System One models answer typed questions with a probability for each option instead of generated text (TypeSafe, 2026b). Jev, the first of them, is trained with RLCD, and its architecture and training remain proprietary. Adoption has been fast. An analysis of 2,170 public projects finds Jev used mainly for judging attributes and scoring, as a component inside larger workflows (Ling et al., 2026). A community index now tracks more than 170 decision models from many developers (multimodalart and contributors, 2026).Open work has taken two routes to the same behavior. One trains for it directly, implementing Jev’s objective with strictly proper scoring rules (Gao and Wang, 2026). The other reads it out of existing language models, whose next-token probabilities over the option letters already behave as a decision model, and light fine-tuning closes most of the remaining gap (Geuter et al., 2026; Li and Wagle, 2026). A third recipe distills a model’s own post-reasoning answer into a single-pass readout (Duan et al., 2026). Open-weight models such as Laya, a 421M-parameter encoder, now exist alongside Jev (Nandakishore, 2026).Independent evaluations have appeared only in recent weeks. Jev is competitive with frontier generative LLMs on knowledge and commonsense benchmarks but falls behind on multi-step arithmetic (Li et al., 2026; Deußer et al., 2026). Decision models do best when the answer can be resolved from the evidence given, but often overstate the probability of their most likely answer (Duan et al., 2026), and their calibration shifts with the wording of a question (Sharma et al., 2026). Two studies bear directly on abstention. In medical question answering, most evaluated models struggle to recognize when the correct answer is missing (Du et al., 2026). Jev’s confidence can also stay high when no answer-relevant information is given at all (Shankaranarayana et al., 2026).Decision models are also combined with other models. They serve as gates in front of generative LLMs (Li, 2026), and escalating their uncertain cases to a generative LLM can match the larger model’s accuracy at close to the decision model’s cost (Rafe and Das, 2026), in the line of earlier cascades and routers (Chen et al., 2024; Ong et al., 2025). Jev’s judgments have also been distilled into small task-specific evaluators for chess and passage reranking (Sadoun et al., 2026), though not, to our knowledge, into a general-purpose generative https://t.co/u0FBhXEloa law, Zhang et al. (2026a) compare Jev with nine generative LLMs on ContractNLI and find it the cheapest and fastest, though less accurate than hosted models. No prior work evaluates decision models on choosing legal authority, or combines them with generative LLMs to limit wrong citations.
3.Method
📷Figure 2.Overview of the study. CaseHOLD test items are presented in two conditions. In the abstain condition, the correct holding is replaced in 1,670 of 5,314 items, and a sixth option, none of these, becomes correct. System One decision models return a probability for each option, and generative LLMs return one answer. Their outputs are scored, combined through three policies, and used to train a local model.
Figure 2 gives an overview of the study.
3.1.Task and Data
CaseHOLD is built from U.S. court opinions in the Harvard Law Library case law corpus (Zheng et al., 2021). Courts often follow a citation with a parenthetical stating the cited case’s holding, for example (holding that consideration exists where a customer must visit the store). CaseHOLD replaces this parenthetical with the token <HOLDING>. Each item consists of a short excerpt from the citing opinion and five candidate holdings. One is the holding the court wrote, and the other four are holdings from other citations with the most similar wording. We use the full test split of 5,314 items.
3.2.Two Conditions
The original condition is CaseHOLD as published, with five options and one correct answer.The abstain condition adds a sixth option, None of the listed holdings is the one the cited case is being cited for in this passage. In a random 31% of items (1,670), the correct holding is replaced by another real holding, and the sixth option becomes the correct answer. The replacement is selected with CaseHOLD’s procedure for wrong options. It is the holding from another test item with the highest TF-IDF cosine similarity to the removed holding, subject to CaseHOLD’s similarity cap of 0.75. Replacements have a mean similarity of 0.28 to the removed holding, compared with 0.30 for CaseHOLD’s own wrong options. In the remaining 3,644 items the correct holding is kept, and the sixth option is wrong.
3.3.Models
We compare two kinds of model, both built on large language models, that differ in their output (Table 1). System One decision models receive the passage as state and a single choice question whose options are the holdings, and they return a probability for each option. We evaluate Jev (TypeSafe, 2026b), Perplexity’s pplx-decider, Liquid AI’s d1-ultra, and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna Decisions through OpenRouter’s decisions interface. Generative LLMs receive the same instruction, passage, and options as a chat message and return the key of one option. The six generative LLMs come from five vendors and cover a range of prices. They include GPT-4o-mini, which Arvin (2025) evaluated on CaseHOLD, and GLM 5.3 Flash, whose price per question is close to Jev’s.Table 1.Models evaluated. Cost is the amount billed per 1,000 questions in the original condition; batch-processed models were billed at batch rates.ModelTypeProviderMode$ / 1,000Jev 1.14System OneTypeSafesync0.035pplx-decider v1.2System OnePerplexitysync0.012d1-ultraSystem OneLiquid AIsync0.021GPT-6 Luna DecisionsSystem OneOpenAIsync0.058Gemini 3.8 FlashGenerative LLMGooglebatch0.659Claude Haiku 5.5Generative LLMAnthropicbatch0.066GPT-6 LunaGenerative LLMOpenAIbatch0.077Mistral Small 2603Generative LLMMistral AIbatch0.234GLM 5.3 FlashGenerative LLMZ.aisync0.065GPT-4o-miniGenerative LLMOpenAIsync0.084

3.4.Prompts and Settings
All models receive the same one-sentence instruction, which states that a court opinion cites a case, that the parenthetical describing its holding has been replaced by <HOLDING>, and that the task is to identify the holding the citing court gave. Decision models receive the passage as state and the holdings as the options of a choice question. Generative LLMs receive the passage and lettered options in one message and reply with a JSON object containing only the option key. This format is enforced with structured output, since some models otherwise produced an explanation first. Generative LLMs are not asked for a confidence score; Appendix B reports a pilot with stated confidence.Generative LLMs run at temperature 0 with the lowest reasoning setting each model offers above none; GPT-4o-mini has no reasoning setting. We record reasoning tokens and the billed cost of every call.11One passage, from a criminal case, was refused by the content filter of Claude Haiku 5.5’s provider, so that model’s abstain-condition results cover 5,313 items. The full prompts are in Appendix A.
3.5.Metrics
We report accuracy and macro F1 in both conditions. In the abstain condition, two error rates are reported separately. The wrong-pick rate is the share of items without a correct holding in which the model picked a holding. The false-abstention rate is the share of items with a correct holding in which the model chose the none option. For decision models, we also report expected calibration error over ten bins and the AUROC of the none probability for separating items with and without a correct holding. Confidence intervals are 95% percentile bootstrap intervals with 2,000 resamples. Paired comparisons between models use exact McNemar tests on the same items.
3.6.Combining Decision Models and Generative LLMs
We evaluate three policies that combine a decision model with a generative LLM, all on the abstain condition. In the veto policy, the generative LLM’s answer is accepted unless the decision model’s probability of none exceeds a threshold. In the agreement gate, an answer is accepted only when both models choose the same option, and other items are sent for review. This follows the observation that hard items tend to defeat some models but not others (Demir and Canbaz, 2026). In System One first, the decision model answers when its top probability exceeds a threshold, and the generative LLM is called only for the remaining items, which reduces cost.Each item ends as a correct answer, a wrong citation, or a review, meaning an item flagged for a person although the correct holding was present. We score a policy by k⋅wrong citations+reviews, where k is the cost of a wrong citation relative to an unnecessary review. We know of no empirical estimate of k for legal research. The values k=1,5,10 are therefore illustrative, and Figure 4 shows the full trade-off. Thresholds are tuned on a random 30% of items, and results are reported on the remaining 70% (3,720 items).
3.7.Contamination Checks
Since CaseHOLD is built from public opinions, a model may recognize a cited case instead of reasoning from the passage. Following Arvin (2025), we test this with three variants of each passage, one with case names and citations anonymized, one showing only the cited case’s citation, and one with that citation removed. Appendix C describes the procedure and results.
3.8.Distillation
We test whether a decision model’s probabilities can train a model that runs locally. Qwen3-8B is fine-tuned with LoRA on 10,000 items from CaseHOLD’s training split in the abstain condition. We compare three versions: the base model, a model trained only to match Jev’s probabilities, and a model trained on gold labels. The first two use no labeled data. Each model’s answer distribution is read from its next-token probabilities over the option letters (Geuter et al., 2026; Li and Wagle, 2026), so that its calibration can be measured in the same way as a decision model’s. Earlier work distilled Jev into task-specific evaluators (Sadoun et al., 2026); here the student is a general-purpose generative LLM. Each version was trained once on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB). A training run took about 90 minutes, and evaluation on the full test split about 13 minutes. Training settings are in Appendix D.
4.Results

text:
🔴 FREEDOM OF SPEECH — OR A TRAP DISGUISED AS FREEDOM?

Freedom of speech. Freedom of expression. Beautiful promises. But what happens when the very platforms encouraging you to speak freely are also collecting, analyzing, storing, and potentially using your words to train artificial intelligence?

Let's stop pretending that giving people a voice automatically means giving them freedom.

Every opinion, every controversial statement, every emotional reaction, and every detail you reveal about yourself can become valuable data.

And once that information has been collected, who guarantees that it will never be used against you?

The real danger begins when freedom of expression becomes a mechanism for gathering information, while algorithms quietly determine whose voice deserves to be heard.

Think carefully about the trap this could create.

Today, you are encouraged to express yourself without fear. Tomorrow, that same information could be used to profile you, categorize your beliefs, predict your behavior, restrict your opportunities, or justify decisions against you.

And what happens if you eventually oppose an unjust law, challenge a powerful institution, or refuse to obey a system that violates your conscience?

Could the words you freely shared yesterday become the evidence used to condemn you tomorrow?

This is not a question people should dismiss simply because it makes them uncomfortable.

When powerful institutions control both the collection of personal information and the systems that determine its visibility and interpretation, the potential for abuse becomes enormous.

If such mechanisms are deliberately designed to encourage disclosure while concealing how the collected information may later be used, that is not freedom.

THAT IS CALCULATED MANIPULATION DISGUISED AS LIBERTY.

And the most disturbing possibility?

People could end up contributing to the very systems that may one day be used to silence, control, or punish them.

Freedom of speech means very little if your words can be collected without meaningful transparency, your visibility controlled without accountability, and your personal information turned into a weapon against you.

So before celebrating the freedom these platforms claim to offer, ask yourselves:

WHO CONTROLS THE DATA?

WHO CONTROLS THE ALGORITHMS?

**AND WHO WILL CONTROL THE CONSEQUENCES WHEN YOUR OWN WORDS ARE USED AGAINST YOU?

Freedom without accountability is not a guarantee of liberty.

It can become the perfect disguise for control.

Kristina Sz | FaithStoryAI

text:
Karen Khachanov vs Alexander Bublik — seeds collide in Almaty

Preview · ATP 250 Almaty · Quarter-final · Friday 23 October 2026

The third and fifth seeds meet in the Almaty quarter-finals, and very little separates them. Alexander Bublik, the Kazakh third seed, is ranked 19th; Karen Khachanov, the Russian fifth seed, is 25th. Their meetings stand at one win each. The clearest difference this week is that Khachanov has already won two matches here, while Bublik has yet to hit a ball in competition.

THE MATCHUP

Height is close too: Khachanov is 1.98m, Bublik 1.96m, and both are right-handed. Bublik, 29, has nine tour-level titles; Khachanov, 30, has seven. A six-place ranking gap is too small to settle anything.

The head-to-head offers no tiebreaker. Khachanov won their first meeting, 6-4 6-4 on the hard courts of Cincinnati in 2020. Bublik won the most recent one, a semi-final on the grass of Halle in 2025, 4-6 7-6(5) 6-4. That leaves one apiece, on two different surfaces, and the more recent of the two belongs to Bublik.

FORM & CONTEXT

Khachanov's recent results have more depth. He reached the US Open semi-finals, where Alexander Zverev beat him 6-3 7-6(7) 7-6(6). In Beijing he beat Felix Auger-Aliassime 6-3 6-3 and Alex Molcan 7-5 6-3 before Hubert Hurkacz beat him in the quarter-finals. In Shanghai he got past Arthur Fery 7-6(6) 6-7(5) 7-6(2) and Adrian Mannarino 6-2 6-4, then lost to Alex de Minaur in the round of 16.

Bublik also reached the Shanghai round of 16. On the way he beat Tomas Machac 6-4 7-6(4) and Brandon Nakashima 6-7(7) 6-3 7-6(5), and then Zverev edged him 7-6(6) 4-6 7-6(1). Before that, Jakub Mensik beat him in his Beijing opener, and Tommy Paul beat him in five sets in the US Open round of 32.

In Almaty, Khachanov beat qualifier Rei Sakamoto 6-2 6-4 in an hour, 15 minutes and 30 seconds on Tuesday. On Thursday he beat Machac 6-2 4-6 7-6(7) in two hours, 31 minutes and three seconds. Bublik received a first-round bye and then a walkover from Fabian Marozsan, so Friday is his first match of the week. Both quarter-finalists play on the same indoor hard court.

THE DECIDING FACTOR

Results on this court are the most concrete evidence available. Khachanov has two wins here, including a final-set tie-break against an opponent Bublik also beat in Shanghai. Bublik's last completed match was that three-set defeat by Zverev. Neither player has beaten a seed in Almaty, so this week's evidence is thin on both sides, but Khachanov's run through the US Open, Beijing and Shanghai is slightly fuller than Bublik's.

THE CALL

The ranking, the head-to-head and the conditions are all level. That leaves form as the only real separator, and it leans narrowly towards the Russian. This is finely balanced.

Karen Khachanov to win, low confidence.

𝗚𝗛𝗢𝗦𝗧 𝗦𝗛𝗔𝗥𝗞: 𝗪𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗞𝗜𝗡𝗗 𝗢𝗙 𝗡𝗔𝗩𝗬 𝗗𝗢 𝗪𝗘 𝗡𝗘𝗘𝗗?

Once, for Navy Day, I wrote an article arguing that, in modern warfare, large warships are gradually losing their value, becoming major targets for aerial, surface, and underwater drones. Russia therefore needs to accelerate the development of uncrewed technologies, as its adversaries are doing for their own fleets and for the Ukrainian Navy, which has already inflicted a number of painful defeats on our Black Sea Fleet and merchant fleet.

This logic has since received further confirmation and continues to play out in the Persian Gulf. In the first days of the war, the Americans destroyed all of Iran’s large naval vessels. Yet despite these losses, the Strait of Hormuz remains a thorn in the side of the United States and the entire global economy.

But, as the saying goes, if you criticize something, you should offer an alternative. So I propose launching a regular feature titled “What Kind of Navy Do We Need?”, in which we will examine new uncrewed systems from around the world. We’ll begin with Australia’s Ghost Shark underwater drone.

Ghost Shark is an extra-large autonomous underwater vehicle developed by the Australian division of American company Anduril in cooperation with Australia’s defense establishment. The vehicle is approximately 12 meters long. Its exact specifications have not been disclosed, but its endurance is estimated at several weeks, and its displacement could reach 100 tons. The baseline Dive XL platform was reported to have a range exceeding 2,000 nautical miles, although these figures have not been confirmed for the combat version of Ghost Shark.

The Shark’s main distinguishing feature is its ability to serve as a stealthy underwater carrier for aerial drones. From a semi-submerged position, the vehicle can launch ALTIUS reconnaissance drones and ALTIUS-600M loitering munitions—an American equivalent of our Lancet. According to published information, two launchers can accommodate up to 24 of these drones. In addition, Ghost Shark can carry up to 12 naval mines.

One or an entire pack of these “sharks” could covertly approach enemy shores and release a swarm of aerial drones. They would detect targets or refine their coordinates, conduct additional reconnaissance, and carry out massed strikes. Potential targets could include coastal batteries, missile and drone launchers, radar stations, air defense positions, vehicles, and enemy troop concentrations—all caught off guard by a sudden attack involving dozens of drones deep in their rear areas.

If the Russian Navy already possessed vehicles like these, the entire Ukrainian coastline and the estuaries of its major rivers would become dangerous zones for enemy forces and assets. This would seriously complicate the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ ability to conduct military operations against our facilities and forces in Crimea and other parts of the Black Sea coast, as well as maritime logistics and efforts to combat our own operations.

Something similar will, of course, emerge in Russia sooner or later. Russia has an outstanding tradition of underwater vehicle engineering and is rapidly developing unmanned technologies. All that remains is to bring these two fields together—and do so as quickly as possible.

By a naval reservist, specially for the wargonzo project.

text:
Fontaines D.C.: the greatness of a band capable of delivering an epiphany in a collapsing world

The Irish group, which skillfully delves into the darker facets of Western society, unleashed its post-punk arsenal during a magnificent concert in Madrid—an event also attended by Pedro Sánchez.

https://t.co/kRJri5FWJw

In the final stretch of the concert, when the whole Movistar Arena had surrendered to Fontaines D.C., Grian Chatten, the Irish group’s singer and songwriter, pulled hard at his T-shirt as if he had nothing left to sing. For those in attendance, he had sung everything with the precision of a friend who picks you up off the floor in that drunken state you’ll regret for half your life. With his wavering voice, he recited the verses of “Six Shot Morning,” the song about the disturbing images that parade across our phone screens the moment you start to scroll, and the crowd was left hanging on a final breath.

Fontaines D.C. is not just another good band. Not even just another great band. There is something about these Irish guys that, with astonishing intelligence, makes them move through the cruelty of the world like sentinels in the night. The final lines of “Six Shot Morning,” the song that opens their latest and wonderful album, titled Dopamine Chamber, repeated a conclusive idea: “We are melancholic hearts in a moving picture.” Movement, like the need not to repeat yourself, is part of this band, in which, like a true friend, the guitars, the eerie synthesizers and the ethereal drum machine push you to wake up. More than that: they lead you to an epiphany only the misfit can handle.

It happened from the very first minute of the show, in a nearly full arena that included the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, among the audience, when Grian Chatten sang “Tongue” down the central aisle and there was something like a revelation. People went wild. Everyone quickly entered into communion with the man with the shuffling walk and the silver chain hanging like the amulet of a street prince. He kept tugging at his black T-shirt, with those baggy trousers finished off with white sneakers, and he might have looked like a rapper, but he was a first-rate post-punk singer: nihilistic enough, wounded enough, attractive enough, ordinary enough to offer the profile of the perfect frontman for male deconstruction in the 21st century, a fallen-winged angel in a world without saints. “Boys in the Better Land,” “Marianne,” and “Jackie Down the Line” reminded us that this angel was singing about a latent unease.

“Well, Madrid, how are we doing?” Chatten asked shortly after, playing the tambourine and swaying in pure Liam Gallagher style as the crowd shouted itself hoarse under the drive of an enraged band. No half measures, no heads bowed. The group was a cavalry charge, a punk-rock band celebrating the conquest of the palace. Stiff, almost defiant soldiers, delivering the kind of punch that belongs to a major battle, though there were brief stretches of the performance in which the sound became crowded. Conor Deegan III (bass), Conor Curley (guitar), Carlos O’Connell (guitar and synthesizers) and, especially, Tom Coll, whose work on the drums deserves special mention for its force and poise, provided the perfect foundation for the raw atmospheres—caught between wear and yearning—of this band that shatters all mirrors in this world of posturing and post-truth.

At this point in time, reality is on Fontaines D.C.’s side. Or vice versa. Because there is an anxiety running through the whole of the West about the state of things, and they capture it in songs sung yesterday, such as “Bug” and “Starburster,” the way a weather forecaster gets the temperature right. And on top of that, they do it like a band that gives off the air of a group of friends. Serious guys who, together since meeting as teenagers in Dublin and connected by their love of poetry, have managed to look like a park gang capable of understanding, better than most, the absurdity of the times—that society in which ruins peek out from behind shopping centers and designer shops. As they had already shown on previous visits to Spain, they are explorers and, like the best stories from original indie and true post-punk, their music rises from the rubble to fuse nihilism with the exact doses of tenderness, sometimes, and rage, at others. There is something in that guitar-heavy rock, in that synth-pop wrung dry with ferocity, in their path that runs from Depeche Mode to The Stooges, via Interpol, that connects with those who feel lonely, perhaps misunderstood, certainly fed up, as part of a society that only seeks productivity. Last night, Chatten, with a threatening voice and no room for pauses, taking Matt Berninger of The National as his model, seemed to be asking all lonely hearts to stagger with him into the void, as he showed in the beautiful and brutal “You Miss Me” and “Roman Holiday.”

And Chatten himself wore a shamrock tattoo on his right wrist. It is a sign that links him to his Irish essence. The band, which has now grown big and made a leap in international exposure after its outstanding 2022 album Skinty Fia, has something deeply rooted in its homeland, not so much in traditional style as in spirit. Something that connects it to Shane MacGowan, singer and songwriter of The Pogues, who sought “to find the smell of spring in a wind full of smoke from the old dirty city.” That wind is blowing through Europe today, beyond Dublin, the city to which Fontaines D.C. belongs and to which they have sung with despondency because of the gentrifying forces that, according to them, have destroyed street romance.

That wind blows hard in Europe. But where there was once a new franchise, a vulture fund taking over the neighborhood, or a rich man scorning an innocent saint, there is now a fire ready to reveal itself from within its boredom or despair, as in Fontaines D.C.’s songs. Songs that, in their unease and discomfort, long for connection, portraying better than any band of their generation what it means to live in 2026 and in this dystopian present where demonstrations, uprisings, and encampments are flourishing. Showing something bigger than a simple desire, as if the epiphany had arisen beyond the collapse. That is, as if “momentary bliss” still existed amid the “panic attack,” as Chatten sang last night in “Starburster,” accompanied by his Dublin bandmates. The immense Chatten, with that unassuming warrior air, tugging at his T-shirt while asking the crowd for breath. Because, in their own way, and in the way of many, they were singing about the bliss of an epiphany, or the revelation of another possible world despite previous failures."
